claim: During vegetative growth, the division septum is formed at the midcell to produce two equal daughter cells in Bacillus subtilis.
source: During vegetative growth, the division septum is formed at the midcell to produce two equal daughter cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the vegetative growth mode of B. subtilis division.

claim: During sporulation, the division septum is formed closer to one pole to yield a smaller forespore and a larger mother cell in Bacillus subtilis.
source: However, during sporulation, the division septum is formed closer to one pole to yield a smaller forespore and a larger mother cell.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the sporulation mode of B. subtilis division.

claim: FtsAZ filaments are present uniformly around the leading edge of the invaginating vegetative septa.
source: While FtsAZ filaments, the major orchestrators of bacterial cell division, are present uniformly around the leading edge of the invaginating vegetative septa, they are only present on the mother cell side of the invaginating sporulation septa.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-ET imaging data shown in the manuscript.

claim: FtsAZ filaments are only present on the mother cell side of the invaginating sporulation septa.
source: While FtsAZ filaments, the major orchestrators of bacterial cell division, are present uniformly around the leading edge of the invaginating vegetative septa, they are only present on the mother cell side of the invaginating sporulation septa.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-ET imaging data shown in the manuscript.

claim: The different distribution and number of FtsAZ filaments impact septal thickness.
source: We provide evidence suggesting that the different distribution and number of FtsAZ filaments impact septal thickness, causing vegetative septa to be thicker than sporulation septa already during constriction.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements and analysis presented in the results.

claim: Vegetative septa are thicker than sporulation septa already during constriction.
source: We provide evidence suggesting that the different distribution and number of FtsAZ filaments impact septal thickness, causing vegetative septa to be thicker than sporulation septa already during constriction.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by thickness measurements from cryo-ET data.

claim: SpoIIE regulates asymmetric divisome localization during sporulation.
source: Finally, we show that a sporulation-specific protein, SpoIIE, regulates asymmetric divisome localization and septal thickness during sporulation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-ET analysis of spoIIE mutants.

claim: SpoIIE regulates septal thickness during sporulation.
source: Finally, we show that a sporulation-specific protein, SpoIIE, regulates asymmetric divisome localization and septal thickness during sporulation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by thickness measurements in spoIIE mutants.

claim: FtsZ polymerizes to form a ring-like structure called the Z-ring at the division site in most bacteria.
source: In most bacteria, cell division is initiated when the tubulin homologue and GTPase, FtsZ, polymerizes to form a ring-like structure, called the Z-ring, at the division site (Bi and Lutkenhaus, 1991; de Boer et al., 1992; Mukherjee and Lutkenhaus, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Z-ring serves as a scaffold onto which about a dozen other proteins assemble to form the divisome.
source: The Z-ring serves as a scaffold onto which about a dozen other proteins assemble to form a mature cell division machinery called 'divisome' (Haeusser and Margolin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, divisome assembly proceeds in two steps.
source: In the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis, divisome assembly proceeds in two steps.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: FtsA is an actin homologue which tethers FtsZ to the membrane via its conserved C-terminal amphipathic helix.
source: One essential protein recruited at this stage is FtsA, an actin homologue which tethers FtsZ to the membrane via its conserved C-terminal amphipathic helix (Pichoff and Lutkenhaus, 2005; Szwedziak et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FtsA can form protofilaments via polymerization in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: FtsA can also form protofilaments via polymerization in an ATP-dependent manner (Szwedziak et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Treadmilling by FtsZ filaments serves as a platform to drive the circumferential motion of septal PG synthases in both B. subtilis and Escherichia coli.
source: Recent studies suggest that treadmilling by FtsZ filaments serves as a platform to drive the circumferential motion of septal PG synthases in both B. subtilis and Escherichia coli, suggesting that this dynamic property of FtsZ filaments can regulate cell wall remodeling in the septal disc (Bisson-Filho et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The medial vegetative septum is almost four times thicker than the polar sporulating septum (~80 nm vs. ~25 nm).
source: Vegetative and sporulating cells differ not only in the positioning of the division site but also in the thickness of their septa, with the medial vegetative septum being almost four times thicker than the polar sporulating septum (~80 nm vs. ~25 nm) (Illing and Errington, 1991; Tocheva et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SpoIIE colocalizes with and directly interacts with FtsZ in sporulating cells.
source: Another distinction is the presence of a membrane protein SpoIIE, which colocalizes with and directly interacts with FtsZ in sporulating cells (Arigoni et al., 1995; Levin et al., 1997; Lucet et al., 2000), but is absent in vegetative cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SpoIIE is absent in vegetative cells.
source: Another distinction is the presence of a membrane protein SpoIIE, which colocalizes with and directly interacts with FtsZ in sporulating cells (Arigoni et al., 1995; Levin et al., 1997; Lucet et al., 2000), but is absent in vegetative cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the absence of SpoIIE in vegetative cells.

claim: SpoIIE localizes only on the forespore side of the sporulation septum at the onset of membrane constriction before being released into the forespore membrane upon septum formation.
source: Recent evidence suggests that SpoIIE localizes only on the forespore side of the sporulation septum at the onset of membrane constriction before being released into the forespore membrane upon septum formation (Carniol et al., 2005; Errington, 2003; Eswaramoorthy et al., 2014; Guberman et al., 2008; Wu et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Certain spoIIE mutants form thicker polar septa compared to wild-type sporangia.
source: Certain spoIIE mutants also form thicker polar septa compared to wild-type sporangia (Barák and Youngman, 1996; Illing and Errington, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two series of electron-dense puncta (dots) are visible at the division site in cryo-ET images of dividing vegetative B. subtilis cells.
source: Our data revealed two series of dots at the division site that were distributed uniformly along the boundary of the leading edge: a membrane-proximal series of dots (~6.5 nm from the invaginating membrane) and a membrane-distal series of dots (~14 nm from the invaginating membrane) (Figure 3A, B, D, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET images shown in Figure 3.

claim: The membrane-proximal series of dots is located ~6.5 nm from the invaginating membrane in vegetative cells.
source: Our data revealed two series of dots at the division site that were distributed uniformly along the boundary of the leading edge: a membrane-proximal series of dots (~6.5 nm from the invaginating membrane) and a membrane-distal series of dots (~14 nm from the invaginating membrane) (Figure 3A, B, D, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET data.

claim: The membrane-distal series of dots is located ~14 nm from the invaginating membrane in vegetative cells.
source: Our data revealed two series of dots at the division site that were distributed uniformly along the boundary of the leading edge: a membrane-proximal series of dots (~6.5 nm from the invaginating membrane) and a membrane-distal series of dots (~14 nm from the invaginating membrane) (Figure 3A, B, D, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET data.

claim: Each series of dots corresponds to filamentous structures of ~3.5 nm diameter arranged next to each other, forming a bundle that spans the circumference of the cell.
source: Rotation of the 3D volume of the tomogram around the short axis of the cell (Figure 2) demonstrated that each series of dots corresponded to filamentous structures of ~3.5 nm diameter arranged next to each other, forming a bundle that spans the circumference of the cell (Figure 3C, E–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by 3D tomogram analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Individual filaments in the membrane-distal series are spaced ~5.5 nm apart.
source: In the membrane-distal series of dots, we could resolve individual filaments spaced ~5.5 nm apart while the filaments corresponding to the membrane-proximal series of dots were more diffuse (Figure 3B, D).
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET images.

claim: The filaments corresponding to the membrane-proximal series of dots are more diffuse than those in the membrane-distal series.
source: In the membrane-distal series of dots, we could resolve individual filaments spaced ~5.5 nm apart while the filaments corresponding to the membrane-proximal series of dots were more diffuse (Figure 3B, D).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET images.

claim: Densities connect the membrane-proximal and the membrane-distal bundles in a ladder-like arrangement in some data sets.
source: In a few data sets, we observed densities that connect the membrane-proximal and the membrane-distal bundles in a ladder-like arrangement (Figure 4, indicated by white lines in Figure 4B, D).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The membrane-distal ring is denser and more continuous than the membrane-proximal ring.
source: Analysis of the intensities of the two rings revealed that the membrane-distal ring is denser and more continuous than the membrane-proximal ring (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by intensity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the FtsZ-linkerQ-rich strain, the distance of the membrane-proximal ring from the invaginating membrane remained unaltered compared to wild type.
source: In B. subtilis FtsZ-linkerQ-rich, the distance of the membrane-proximal ring from the invaginating membrane remained unaltered compared to wild type, while the membrane-distal filaments were further from the membrane compared to wild type (17.5 ± 1.1 nm vs. 14 ± 0.6 nm) with a wide distribution ranging from ~15 to ~19 nm (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), establishing the membrane-distal filaments to be FtsZ.
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the FtsZ-linkerQ-rich strain, the membrane-distal filaments are further from the membrane compared to wild type (17.5 ± 1.1 nm vs. 14 ± 0.6 nm).
source: In B. subtilis FtsZ-linkerQ-rich, the distance of the membrane-proximal ring from the invaginating membrane remained unaltered compared to wild type, while the membrane-distal filaments were further from the membrane compared to wild type (17.5 ± 1.1 nm vs. 14 ± 0.6 nm) with a wide distribution ranging from ~15 to ~19 nm (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), establishing the membrane-distal filaments to be FtsZ.
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The membrane-distal filaments are FtsZ.
source: In B. subtilis FtsZ-linkerQ-rich, the distance of the membrane-proximal ring from the invaginating membrane remained unaltered compared to wild type, while the membrane-distal filaments were further from the membrane compared to wild type (17.5 ± 1.1 nm vs. 14 ± 0.6 nm) with a wide distribution ranging from ~15 to ~19 nm (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), establishing the membrane-distal filaments to be FtsZ.
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated and supported by the FtsZ-linkerQ-rich experiment.

claim: The membrane-proximal ring is composed of FtsA filaments.
source: We assigned the identity of the membrane-proximal ring to be FtsA filaments as no other cell division proteins form filaments in vivo or in vitro and its distance to the membrane is comparable to that of FtsA filaments in E. coli upon overexpression (Szwedziak et al., 2014).
evidence: This assignment is stated and supported by comparison to E. coli data and the process of elimination.

claim: The more continuous membrane-distal ring of FtsZ filaments is tethered to the membrane via a patchy membrane-proximal ring of FtsA filaments.
source: Thus, we conclude that the more continuous membrane-distal ring of FtsZ filaments is tethered to the membrane via a patchy membrane-proximal ring of FtsA filaments (Figure 5C, Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated and supported by the cryo-ET data and FtsZ-linkerQ-rich experiments.

claim: The Z-ring is mostly continuous in the cellular sections imaged by cryo-FIB-ET during vegetative growth.
source: Our cryo-FIB-ET data indicated that the Z-ring was mostly continuous in the cellular sections we imaged. We observed fairly continuous Z-rings in 9 out of 16 tomograms of dividing vegetative cells that we captured (Figures 3C, E and 4C, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and supported by multiple tomograms.

claim: Two series of dots are visible only on the mother cell side of the leading edge of the invaginating sporulation septum.
source: Next, we analyzed divisome architecture in sporulating B. subtilis cells. During sporulation, the division site shifts closer to a pole as opposed to medial division during vegetative growth (Figure 1). We again observed two series of dots in dividing sporulating cells, but remarkably, they were visible only on the mother cell side of the leading edge of the invaginating sporulation septum (Figure 7A–C, Figure 7—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET images shown in Figure 7.

claim: The membranes at the leading edge of the nascent septum in sporulating cells are not as defined as in vegetative cells.
source: Of note, the membranes at the leading edge of the nascent septum in sporulating cells were not as defined as in vegetative cells, suggesting that they have a higher ratio of protein to membrane, as might be expected due to the presence of both transmembrane cell division proteins and sporulation-specific multipass transmembrane proteins (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and an explanation is provided based on protein composition.

claim: FtsAZ filaments mediating cell division localize differently during vegetative growth and sporulation.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that FtsAZ filaments mediating cell division localize differently during vegetative growth and sporulation. During vegetative growth, they span the leading edge of the invaginating septum uniformly, whereas during sporulation they localize only on the mother cell side (Figure 7D).
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET data comparing vegetative and sporulating cells.

claim: The thickness of the invaginating septa in vegetative cells is ~50 ± 3 nm.
source: Our data showed that the thickness of the invaginating septa in vegetative cells was ~50 ± 3 nm compared to ~80 nm when the septum formation is completed (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The thickness of the vegetative septum upon closure is ~80 nm.
source: Our data showed that the thickness of the invaginating septa in vegetative cells was ~50 ± 3 nm compared to ~80 nm when the septum formation is completed (Figure 7E, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The thickness of the invaginating septa in sporulating cells is ~25 ± 2.5 nm.
source: On the other hand, the thickness of the invaginating septa in sporulating cells was almost half of that of vegetative cells (~25 ± 2.5 nm, Figure 7E) during constriction.
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The thickness of the sporulation septum upon closure is ~23 nm.
source: Our previous results demonstrate that the thickness of the sporulation septum upon closure is ~23 nm (Khanna et al., 2019), close to the observed thickness of the invaginating sporulation septa (Figure 7E).
evidence: This measurement is stated and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The sporulation septum does not thicken upon closure.
source: Hence, contrary to the vegetative septum, the sporulation septum does not thicken upon closure.
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated based on comparison of invaginating and closed septum thicknesses.

claim: The thickening of vegetative septa upon closure might be related to the expansion of the cell wall due to PG hydrolysis during cell separation.
source: This further supports the idea that the thickening of vegetative septa upon closure might be related to the expansion of the cell wall due to PG hydrolysis during cell separation.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the observation that vegetative septa thicken upon closure.

claim: The mother cell and the forespore do not separate after septation.
source: The mother cell and the forespore do not separate after septation, and therefore the cell wall hydrolases that participate in splitting of the two daughter cells during vegetative growth would not participate in the same capacity during sporulation.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological process during sporulation.

claim: Even at the onset of cell division the sporulating septum is thinner than the vegetative septum.
source: Our results, therefore, suggest that even at the onset of cell division the sporulating septum is thinner than the vegetative septum.
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated based on measurements of invaginating septa.

claim: FtsZ bundles span approximately twice the length in vegetative cells compared to sporulating cells (~51 ± 2.9 nm vs. ~27 ± 3.6 nm).
source: On average, FtsZ bundles spanned twice the length in vegetative cells compared to sporulating cells (~51 ± 2.9 nm vs. ~27 ± 3.6 nm, Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 2), indicating that there are twice as many FtsZ filaments participating in cell division during vegetative growth as compared to sporulation.
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: There are twice as many FtsZ filaments participating in cell division during vegetative growth as compared to sporulation.
source: On average, FtsZ bundles spanned twice the length in vegetative cells compared to sporulating cells (~51 ± 2.9 nm vs. ~27 ± 3.6 nm, Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 2), indicating that there are twice as many FtsZ filaments participating in cell division during vegetative growth as compared to sporulation.
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated based on the measurement of FtsZ bundle length.

claim: The sporulation septum being thinner than the vegetative septum is likely a consequence of fewer FtsZ filaments tracking the division plane during sporulation.
source: Based on these data, and the fact that the dynamic property of FtsZ filaments regulates the insertion of the cell wall material during septal biogenesis (Bisson-Filho et al., 2017; Squyres et al., 2020), we propose that the sporulation septum being thinner than the vegetative septum is likely a consequence of fewer FtsZ filaments tracking the division plane during sporulation.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the data and previous literature.

claim: Divisome architecture in spoIIE null mutant sporangia is similar to that in vegetative cells, with two series of dots corresponding to FtsAZ filaments present uniformly along the leading edge of the invaginating septum.
source: Surprisingly, we noted that divisome architecture in spoIIE is similar to that in vegetative cells, with two series of dots corresponding to FtsAZ filaments present uniformly along the leading edge of the invaginating septum, in contrast to wild-type sporangia where they were present only on the mother cell side (Figure 8A–C, N).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and supported by cryo-ET images shown in Figure 8.

claim: The invaginating sporulation septum in spoIIE sporangia is ~42 ± 4 nm thick.
source: Also, at ~42 ± 4 nm, the invaginating sporulation septum in spoIIE sporangia was comparable in thickness to the invaginating vegetative septum, implicating SpoIIE in regulating both the localization of FtsAZ filaments and the septal thickness during sporulation (Figure 8O, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This measurement is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 8O.

claim: SpoIIE regulates both the localization of FtsAZ filaments and the septal thickness during sporulation.
source: Also, at ~42 ± 4 nm, the invaginating sporulation septum in spoIIE sporangia was comparable in thickness to the invaginating vegetative septum, implicating SpoIIE in regulating both the localization of FtsAZ filaments and the septal thickness during sporulation (Figure 8O, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated based on the spoIIE mutant analysis.

claim: There may be other unidentified factors in addition to SpoIIE that regulate the thickness of the sporulation septum.
source: This suggests that there may be other unidentified factors in addition to SpoIIE that regulate the thickness of the sporulation septum.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that spoIIE sporulation septa are still slightly thinner than vegetative septa.

claim: Both the transmembrane and the FtsZ-binding domains of SpoIIE are essential to regulate the localization of FtsAZ filaments and septal thickness during sporulation.
source: Our cryo-FIB-ET data demonstrated that the organization of FtsAZ filaments at the polar septum and the septal thickness in all the three mutant strains is similar to spoIIE sporangia (Figure 8D–O, Figure 8—figure supplements 3 and 4, Figure 8—video 1). These data indicate that both the transmembrane and the FtsZ-binding domains of SpoIIE are essential to regulate the localization of FtsAZ filaments and septal thickness during sporulation.
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated based on analysis of spoIIE domain deletion mutants.

claim: SpoIIE is present exclusively on the forespore side of the septum even before the onset of membrane constriction.
source: SpoIIE is present exclusively on the forespore side of the septum even before the onset of membrane constriction (Eswaramoorthy et al., 2014; Guberman et al., 2008; Wu et al., 1998), and our data show that both the membrane-spanning and the FtsZ-binding domains of SpoIIE mediate differential localization of FtsAZ filaments during sporulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interaction of SpoIIE with FtsZ may disrupt the interaction of FtsA with FtsZ on the forespore side.
source: Hence, we hypothesized that the interaction of SpoIIE with FtsZ may disrupt the interaction of FtsA with FtsZ on the forespore side.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the asymmetric localization of FtsAZ.

claim: SpoIIE may cause the disassociation of residual FtsA filaments from the divisome in the forespore so that cytokinesis exclusively proceeds from the mother cell side.
source: It is possible that SpoIIE causes the disassociation of these residual FtsA filaments from the divisome in the forespore as SpoIIE is only present on the forespore side of the invaginating septum so that cytokinesis exclusively proceeds from the mother cell side (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on fluorescence microscopy observations.

claim: During vegetative growth, two cytoskeletal rings localize uniformly around the leading edge of the invaginating medial septum to orchestrate cell division.
source: First, we show that during vegetative growth, two cytoskeletal rings localize uniformly around the leading edge of the invaginating medial septum to orchestrate cell division, a membrane-proximal ring of FtsA filaments that tethers the membrane-distal ring of FtsZ filaments to the membrane (Figures 3–6).
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion supported by the results shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: During the asymmetrically positioned division event at the onset of sporulation, FtsAZ filaments are assembled only on the mother cell side of the invaginating polar septum.
source: Second, we demonstrate that during the asymmetrically positioned division event in the cell at the onset of sporulation, FtsAZ filaments are assembled only on the mother cell side of the invaginating polar septum (Figure 7A–D), demonstrating a surprising degree of asymmetry even in the localization of the division machinery.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion supported by the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: During septal biogenesis the number of FtsAZ filaments tracking the sporulation septum is approximately half of that in the vegetative septum, which likely gives rise to a thinner sporulation septum.
source: Third, our data suggest that during septal biogenesis the number of FtsAZ filaments tracking the sporulation septum is approximately half of that in the vegetative septum, which likely gives rise to a thinner sporulation septum by mediating the circumferential motion of fewer PG synthases around the division plane during sporulation (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion supported by the results shown in Figure 7.

claim: SpoIIE is essential for the asymmetric assembly of FtsAZ filaments and septal thickness at the onset of sporulation.
source: Finally, we show that a sporulation-specific protein SpoIIE, which is essential for cell-specific gene expression after polar septation, is also essential for the asymmetric assembly of FtsAZ filaments and septal thickness at the onset of sporulation (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion supported by the results shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The sporulation septum is both asymmetrically positioned in the cell and assembled by an asymmetrically localized division machinery.
source: These results demonstrate that the sporulation septum is both asymmetrically positioned in the cell and that it is assembled by an asymmetrically localized division machinery.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion in the Discussion based on the results presented.

claim: Only a single cytoskeleton ring of FtsZ was observed using cryo-ET in Gram-negative bacteria including E. coli and C. crescentus.
source: Previously, only a single cytoskeleton ring of FtsZ was observed using cryo-ET in Gram-negative bacteria including E. coli and C. crescentus (Li et al., 2007; Szwedziak et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two rings corresponding to FtsA and FtsZ filaments are observed in cryo-FIB-ET images of B. subtilis during both vegetative growth and sporulation.
source: However, we observed two rings corresponding to FtsA and FtsZ filaments in cryo-FIB-ET images of B. subtilis during both vegetative growth and sporulation, even though the ratio of FtsZ to FtsA is same (5:1) in B. subtilis and E. coli and there are enough molecules of FtsA to form a circumferential A-ring in both species (Feucht et al., 2001; Rueda et al., 2003).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and contrasts with observations in Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: The ratio of FtsZ to FtsA is 5:1 in both B. subtilis and E. coli.
source: However, we observed two rings corresponding to FtsA and FtsZ filaments in cryo-FIB-ET images of B. subtilis during both vegetative growth and sporulation, even though the ratio of FtsZ to FtsA is same (5:1) in B. subtilis and E. coli and there are enough molecules of FtsA to form a circumferential A-ring in both species (Feucht et al., 2001; Rueda et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An A-ring appears more patchy compared to the mostly continuous Z-ring in B. subtilis.
source: But an A-ring is apparent only in B. subtilis, although it appears more patchy as compared to the mostly continuous Z-ring.
evidence: This observation is directly stated based on the cryo-ET data.

claim: Cell division in B. subtilis involves the constriction of a septal disc composed of thicker septal PG (~25 nm during sporulation and ~50 nm during vegetative growth) than in E. coli or C. crescentus, where the septal disc consists of only ~4-nm-thick PG.
source: One possible explanation for this difference between species is that cell division in B. subtilis involves the constriction of a septal disc composed of thicker septal PG (~25 nm during sporulation and ~50 nm during vegetative growth) than in E. coli or C. crescentus, where the septal disc consists of only ~4-nm-thick PG.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the difference in divisome architecture between species.

claim: Cytokinesis in B. subtilis may require more FtsA filaments in order to tether the increased number of PG synthetases that are required to build a thicker septum during constriction.
source: Hence, cytokinesis in B. subtilis may require more FtsA filaments in order to tether the increased number of PG synthetases that are required to build a thicker septum during constriction.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for why an A-ring is visible in B. subtilis but not in Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: The lateral spacing between FtsZ filaments is decreased in B. subtilis (~5.5 nm) compared to E. coli and C. crescentus (6.5–8 nm).
source: Other differences between our data and that from Gram-negative bacteria are the decreased lateral spacing between FtsZ filaments (~5.5 nm in B. subtilis vs. 6.5–8 nm in E. coli and C. crescentus), and the shorter distances of the Z-ring and the A-ring from the membrane (~14 nm and ~6.5 nm, respectively, in B. subtilis vs. ~16 nm and ~8 nm, respectively, in E. coli).
evidence: This comparison is directly stated based on the current data and previous studies.

claim: The distances of the Z-ring and the A-ring from the membrane are shorter in B. subtilis (~14 nm and ~6.5 nm, respectively) compared to E. coli (~16 nm and ~8 nm, respectively).
source: Other differences between our data and that from Gram-negative bacteria are the decreased lateral spacing between FtsZ filaments (~5.5 nm in B. subtilis vs. 6.5–8 nm in E. coli and C. crescentus), and the shorter distances of the Z-ring and the A-ring from the membrane (~14 nm and ~6.5 nm, respectively, in B. subtilis vs. ~16 nm and ~8 nm, respectively, in E. coli).
evidence: This comparison is directly stated based on the current data and previous studies.

claim: A tighter bundling of FtsAZ filaments with each other and with the membrane in B. subtilis may be necessary for the synthesis of the thick septal PG.
source: It is possible that a tighter bundling of FtsAZ filaments with each other and with the membrane in B. subtilis may be necessary for the synthesis of the thick septal PG.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed differences in filament spacing and distances.

claim: The Z-ring is mostly continuous during vegetative growth, similar to previous cryo-ET studies in E. coli and C. crescentus.
source: Our result that the Z-ring is mostly continuous during vegetative growth is similar to a previous cryo-ET study that also revealed the continuity of Z-rings in both E. coli and C. crescentus (Szwedziak et al., 2014).
evidence: This comparison is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: In super-resolution microscopy, the Z-ring in both B. subtilis and E. coli appeared patchy with regions of low fluorescence intensity that may indicate gaps in the ring.
source: However, this contrasts with super-resolution microscopy in which the Z-ring in both B. subtilis and E. coli appeared patchy with regions of low fluorescence intensity that may indicate gaps in the ring (Holden et al., 2014; Strauss et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous super-resolution microscopy studies.

claim: Cryo-ET has better spatial resolution than super-resolution microscopy and enables visualization of cellular structures in a near-native state.
source: We note that cryo-ET has better spatial resolution than super-resolution microscopy and enables visualization of cellular structures in a near-native state.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of cryo-ET as a technique.

claim: A thinner septum could facilitate interaction between protein complex subunits located in the forespore and those in the mother cell during sporulation.
source: A thinner septum could be beneficial during sporulation in two ways. First, several protein complexes are proposed to form channels across both septal membranes during sporulation, including SpoIIQ-SpoIIIAH and SpoIIIE (Blaylock et al., 2004; Fleming et al., 2010; Meisner et al., 2008; Riley et al., 2021a; Yen Shin et al., 2015). A thinner septum could facilitate interaction between the subunits located in the forespore and those in the mother cell.
evidence: This is a proposed benefit of a thinner septum supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A thinner septum may facilitate the phagocytosis-like process of engulfment during sporulation.
source: Second, a thinner septum may facilitate the phagocytosis-like process of engulfment, during which migration of the mother cell membrane is driven by the remodeling of the junction between the septal PG and the lateral PG via the coordinated synthesis and degradation of the septal PG (Khanna et al., 2019; Ojkic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed benefit of a thinner septum supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Asymmetric distribution of FtsAZ to the mother cell side of the septum may allow enough FtsAZ complexes to remain in the mother cell to support a second division site at the opposite cell pole as a backup.
source: In addition to facilitating the formation of a thinner septum, asymmetric distribution of FtsAZ to the mother cell side of the septum may also be beneficial for other downstream events during sporulation. First, it is possible that such a strategy allows enough FtsAZ complexes to remain in the mother cell to support a second division site at the opposite cell pole as a backup should the first septum be misassembled or fail to support the onset of cell-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is a proposed benefit of asymmetric FtsAZ distribution.

claim: The second polar division site is dissolved after the onset of cell-specific gene expression by either the PG degradation complex SpoIIDMP or MciZ in the mother cell.
source: This second polar division site is dissolved after the onset of cell-specific gene expression by either the PG degradation complex SpoIIDMP (Abanes-De Mello et al., 2002; Eichenberger et al., 2001; Pogliano et al., 1999) or MciZ (Bisson-Filho et al., 2015; Handler et al., 2008) in the mother cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ensuring that the forespore does not harbor active cytoskeletal filaments upon septation could provide an additional safety mechanism to prevent aberrant cell division events in the forespore.
source: Second, if FtsAZ complexes were present on the forespore side of the septum after septation, they may induce aberrant cell division events in the small forespore if their activity was not efficiently inhibited by the Min and the nucleoid occlusion proteins (Marston et al., 1998; Wu and Errington, 2004). Thus, ensuring that the forespore does not harbor active cytoskeletal filaments upon septation could provide an additional safety mechanism.
evidence: This is a proposed benefit of asymmetric FtsAZ distribution supported by citations.

claim: Just after polar septation there is some FtsAZ signal in the forespore that gradually diminishes as engulfment proceeds.
source: Time-lapse microscopy of FtsA-mNeonGreen and FtsZ-mNeonGreen indicated that just after polar septation there was some FtsAZ signal in the forespore that gradually diminished as engulfment proceeded in these cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is directly stated and supported by time-lapse microscopy data.

claim: There may be protein(s) in the forespore that mediate degradation of FtsAZ polymers that do not participate in cell division yet remain in the forespore.
source: It is possible that there are protein(s) in the forespore that mediate degradation of FtsAZ polymers that do not participate in cell division yet remain in the forespore, ensuring an extra layer of safety mechanism to prevent any aberrant cell division events in the forespore.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of diminishing FtsAZ signal in the forespore.

claim: Certain proteins involved in central carbon metabolism and metabolic precursor synthesis were depleted specifically in the forespore after polar septation.
source: A recent study from the lab showed that certain proteins involved in central carbon metabolism and metabolic precursor synthesis were depleted specifically in the forespore after polar septation (Riley et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: PG synthases, including Pbp2B, preferentially localize to the forespore side of the leading edge of the engulfing membrane.
source: Finally, we have previously shown that PG synthases, including Pbp2B, a component of the divisome, preferentially localize to the forespore side of the leading edge of the engulfing membrane (Khanna et al., 2019; Ojkic et al., 2016), where they act together with the mother cell PG degradation complex SpoIIDMP to mediate the coordinated synthesis and degradation of the cell wall to drive engulfment membrane migration (Ojkic et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Asymmetric cell division is a common developmental theme in eukaryotes to generate progeny with diverse cellular fates.
source: Asymmetric cell division is a common developmental theme in eukaryotes to generate progeny with diverse cellular fates (Li, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In B. subtilis sporulation, an axis of polarity is likely established when the division plane shifts from medial to polar position.
source: In case of B. subtilis sporulation, an axis of polarity is likely established when the division plane shifts from medial to polar position and cell fate determinants are differentially distributed between the future forespore and the mother cell compartments at the onset of membrane constriction.
evidence: This is a statement about the establishment of polarity during sporulation.

claim: SpoIIE is a cell fate determinant that restricts FtsAZ filaments to the mother cell side of the asymmetrically positioned septum.
source: In this study, we have identified SpoIIE as a cell fate determinant that also restricts FtsAZ filaments to the mother cell side of the asymmetrically positioned septum, likely by its preferential localization to the forespore side of the invaginating septum (Eswaramoorthy et al., 2014; Guberman et al., 2008; Wu et al., 1998).
evidence: This conclusion is directly stated based on the results and supported by citations.

claim: Region III of SpoIIE consists of a phosphatase domain that is essential to activate σF in the forespore by dephosphorylating SpoIIAA after septum closure.
source: Region III, C-terminal part of SpoIIE, consists of a phosphatase domain that is essential to activate σF in the forespore by dephosphorylating SpoIIAA after septum closure.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of region III of SpoIIE.

claim: A SpoIIE mutant that is enzymatically inactive in dephosphorylating SpoIIA (D746A substitution) behaved similar to wild type with respect to polar septation during sporulation.
source: It was previously shown that a SpoIIE mutant that is enzymatically inactive in dephosphorylating SpoIIA (D746A substitution) behaved similar to wild type with respect to polar septation during sporulation (Carniol et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Missense mutations spoIIE64 and spoIIE71 that map to region III of SpoIIE and affect its phosphatase activity were shown to have thin polar septa.
source: In another study, missense mutations spoIIE64 and spoIIE71 that map to region III of SpoIIE and affect its phosphatase activity were shown to have thin polar septa in thin-section electron microscopy images (Barák and Youngman, 1996), suggesting that the phosphatase activity of SpoIIE likely does not affect the septal thickness.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.
